title: Safe-drinking-water investment can reduce pollution and older-adult mortality while household exposure remains separate
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35288; drinking-water pollution readings, water systems/areas, Safe Drinking Water Act loans, and linked administrative Medicare outcomes for older Americans
geography: United States; 48 states, national and place-level water-quality measures, and older-American health outcomes

observations.period: 2003-2019; drinking-water pollution trend and place differences

pollution_above_current_standards.unit: share of readings above current health standards

pollutants_covered.unit: pollutants measured over the study period

population_reaching_standards.value: about 10%-20% of Americans still receive drinking water that violates standards

observations.method: The authors assemble water-quality readings obtained from 48 states through Freedom of Information Act and related requests, measure trends and place differences, and link pollution measures to administrative Medicare data for older Americans.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract reports broad trends and socioeconomic patterns but does not provide a household-level exposure measure, a complete explanation for every place difference, or a measure of each household's water use, treatment, or private spending.
observations.subgroup: Water-quality readings and areas; low-income areas show higher pollution, while Black and Hispanic communities have more complex patterns in the study's reported comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: A fall in the share of readings above standards can coexist with persistent local hotspots, unregulated pollutants, different monitoring intensity, or unequal ability to avoid exposure; an area comparison is not a household harm estimate.

observations.period: Study period; Safe Drinking Water Act loan effects

denominator.unit: water-system loan observations and linked older-American Medicare outcomes; study-specific denominator not stated in the abstract

safe_drinking_water_act_loans.unit: estimated loan effect on drinking-water pollution

older_american_mortality.unit: estimated loan effect on mortality rates of older Americans

estimated_cost_to_remove_excess_pollutio.unit: dollars per person per year at the estimated average loan cost-effectiveness

observations.method: The paper estimates the effect of Safe Drinking Water Act loans on water pollution and links pollution to administrative Medicare outcomes; the authors report both pollution and mortality reductions and a cost-effectiveness estimate.
observations.uncertainty: This is a working paper and has not been peer-reviewed by the NBER Board. The abstract does not establish which individual households received a loan-funded improvement, their exposure or treatment, or whether the estimated cost applies uniformly across places.
observations.subgroup: Water systems and older Americans represented in linked Medicare outcomes; the result is not a same-household panel from exposure through later health, spending, trust, or political action.
observations.counterinterpretation: Loan effects may vary with system capacity, baseline pollution, implementation, local conditions, and the pollutants measured; average mortality effects do not prove that every funded system or household improved equally.

related_sources.claim: The working-paper PDF provides the authors' methods, estimates, tables, and limitations behind the abstract.

boundary: This record adds a measured place-to-health and public-loan result: pollution declined, loans reduced pollution, and linked older-American mortality fell in the study's estimates. It does not follow the same household from exposure through bottled-water or filter spending, home value, health care, trust, political action, or durable local acceptance.
